lead: Concept learning learns a rule from labelled examples. Each example is a row of attribute values marked positive or negative. The learner searches a space of possible rules for one that covers all positives and rejects all negatives. This chapter studies three standard tools: Find-S, version spaces and candidate elimination. They are used in small logical learning problems and as the basis for later rule learners. The ideas explain how a machine can move from examples to a general rule, and why the choice of hypothesis language limits what it can learn.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for hypothesis space and learning as search, and Chapter 1.5 for sets and basic probability intuition.

blocks.text: Concept learning takes a set of examples, each described by attribute values and marked positive or negative, and produces a rule that separates them. The rule is the target concept. In this chapter an example is a row with three attributes: Sky, Temp, Wind. A positive example belongs to the concept; a negative example does not.

Let X be the set of examples and C:X→{0,1} the target concept. A hypothesis h is a conjunction of constraints, one per attribute. A constraint is a fixed value, ? (any value), or ∅ (no value allowed). h covers x when every attribute matches. ? matches any value; ∅ matches no value. The hypothesis space H is all such conjunctions. For three attributes with small domains H is finite, so learning is search through H.

General-to-specific ordering: h1 is more general than h2 exactly when h1 covers every example that h2 covers. Replacing a fixed value or ∅ by ? makes that hypothesis more general. Do not compare hypotheses by counting ?; two hypotheses with different numbers of ? can be incomparable. The all-? hypothesis ⊤ covers everything. The all-∅ hypothesis ⊥ covers nothing. Find-S and candidate elimination both use this order.

Find-S starts at the most specific hypothesis h=(∅,∅,∅). For each positive example, if h covers it, leave h unchanged. If not, replace each conflicting fixed value by ?. For each negative example, do nothing. Return h after all positives.

items: For each positive x: for each attribute a, if h[a]=∅ set it to x[a]; if h[a]≠x[a] set it to ?.
For each negative example: skip it.

blocks.text: Example: positives (Sunny,Warm,Strong) and (Sunny,Warm,Weak) give h=(Sunny,Warm,?) after the second example. The negatives (Rainy,Cold,Strong) and (Sunny,Cold,Strong) do not change h. Find-S returns one most specific hypothesis covering all positive examples. It is consistent with all examples only when a consistent conjunction exists, that is, when there is no noise and the hypothesis language is adequate. Find-S does not check negatives, so its answer can still cover a negative example if those conditions fail.

A version space is the set of all hypotheses in H that cover every positive example and no negative example. It is represented by two boundary sets. S is the set of most specific hypotheses in the version space. G is the set of most general hypotheses. Every consistent hypothesis lies between some s in S and some g in G under the general-to-specific order.

Candidate elimination updates S and G example by example. For a positive example x: remove from G every hypothesis that does not cover x; generalize each s in S minimally so that it covers x; remove from S any hypothesis more general than another member of S. For a negative example x: remove from S every hypothesis that covers x. For each g in G that covers x, replace g with all minimal specializations that exclude x and remain consistent with the positives, then prune G. If g already excludes x, leave it.

List-then-eliminate is the brute-force version: list all h in H, keep those consistent with every example. It gives the same version space but costs time proportional to |H|. Candidate elimination can be cheaper because it stores only the boundaries. Some syllabi use the phrase candidate elimination for the boundary update itself. If S or G becomes empty, no hypothesis in H fits the data.

figure.caption: Candidate elimination on the worked example: S is filled in by the first positive and generalizes only once, at P2, then never moves, while each negative example trims G until only (?,Warm,?) survives. The last row is the final answer, and its S is the same hypothesis that Find-S returns.

spec.title: Candidate elimination, worked example
spec.aria: Five stacked steps of candidate elimination on the worked example: S starts as (∅,∅,∅) and G as (?,?,?); P1 makes S (Sunny,Warm,Strong), P2 generalizes S to (Sunny,Warm,?); N1 splits G into (Sunny,?,?) and (?,Warm,?); N2 leaves S at (Sunny,Warm,?) and G at (?,Warm,?).

examples.question: Attributes: Sky, Temp, Wind. Positive examples: P1=(Sunny,Warm,Strong), P2=(Sunny,Warm,Weak). Negative examples: N1=(Rainy,Cold,Strong), N2=(Sunny,Cold,Strong). Run Find-S. Run candidate elimination. State final S and G and the number of hypotheses in each boundary set.
steps: P2: Wind differs (Strong vs Weak), so h2=(Sunny,Warm,?).
N1 and N2 are negative, so h stays (Sunny,Warm,?). Final Find-S hypothesis: h=(Sunny,Warm,?).
Candidate elimination starts with S0={(∅,∅,∅)} and G0={(?,?,?)}.
N1: S2 does not cover N1, so S stays. Remove (?,?,?) from G. Minimal specializations covering both positives and excluding N1 are (Sunny,?,?) and (?,Warm,?). G3={(Sunny,?,?), (?,Warm,?)}.

N2: S2 does not cover N2, so S stays. (?,Warm,?) does not cover N2, so it stays. (Sunny,?,?) covers N2; replace it by (Sunny,Warm,?). Prune (Sunny,Warm,?) because (?,Warm,?) is more general. G4={(?,Warm,?)}.
Final S={(Sunny,Warm,?)} and G={(?,Warm,?)}. Number in S=1. Number in G=1.
examples.answer: Final Find-S hypothesis is (Sunny,Warm,?); final S=(Sunny,Warm,?) with one hypothesis; final G=(?,Warm,?) with one hypothesis.
examples.check:
P=[('Sunny','Warm','Strong'),('Sunny','Warm','Weak')]
N=[('Rainy','Cold','Strong'),('Sunny','Cold','Strong')]
S=[('Sunny','Warm','?')]
G=[('?','Warm','?')]
def covers(h,x):
    return all(a=='?' or a==v for a,v in zip(h,x))
assert all(covers(h,p) for h in S+G for p in P)
assert all(not covers(h,n) for h in S+G for n in N)
print(len(S))
print(len(G))

traps: Positive examples mainly generalize S and also filter G; negative examples mainly specialize G and also filter S. A negative example covered by an S hypothesis removes that S hypothesis.
? matches any value; ∅ matches no value. They are not the same, and ∅ is not a missing value.
Find-S ignores negatives, so do not claim it always rejects all negatives.
In G, specializing means replacing ? by a value or ∅; adding ? makes a hypothesis more general, not more specific.
If S or G is empty, the version space is empty; do not invent a boundary hypothesis.

quiz.q: What do ? and ∅ mean in a hypothesis?
quiz.a: ? matches any value of that attribute. ∅ matches no value, so the hypothesis cannot cover an example with any value there.

quiz.q: Why does Find-S ignore negative examples?
quiz.a: Find-S only generalizes the current hypothesis from positives. It has no step for rejecting a negative, so its final hypothesis may cover one.

quiz.q: Use P1=(Sunny,Warm,Strong) and P2=(Sunny,Warm,Weak). Give the Find-S hypothesis after P2.
quiz.a: Start (∅,∅,∅); after P1 (Sunny,Warm,Strong); after P2 Wind differs, so h=(Sunny,Warm,?).

quiz.q: In the worked example, what are S and G after N1?
A negative example is covered by s in S. What does candidate elimination do?
quiz.a: Remove from S every hypothesis that covers that negative example. For each g in G that covers it, replace g by all minimal specializations that exclude the example and remain consistent with the positives; then prune G.

quiz.q: Why can candidate elimination end with empty G?
quiz.a: No hypothesis in H is both general enough to cover all positives and specific enough to reject all negatives. The data or the hypothesis language is too restrictive.
List-then-eliminate tests every h in H and keeps consistent ones. Candidate elimination stores only the S and G boundaries and updates them; both give the same version space.
The set of all hypotheses in H that cover every positive example and no negative example.

beyond: Not for the exam. Version spaces appear in active learning, where the learner keeps all consistent rules and chooses the next query that halves the version space. Modern systems often replace exact version spaces with probabilistic beliefs or neural hypotheses. Search for 'version space active learning' and 'candidate elimination algorithm'.
